claim: The HIV/AIDS epidemic affects more than 37 million individuals worldwide, and there were 2 million new infections in 2014.
source: The HIV/AIDS epidemic affects more than 37 million individuals worldwide, and there were 2 million new infections in 2014 (Deeks et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deeks et al., 2015

claim: Less than half of the persons diagnosed with HIV remain in care in the United States.
source: but less than half of the persons diagnosed with HIV remain in care in the United States.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript, likely based on established knowledge

claim: One major obstacle to developing a universal vaccine is the high mutability of HIV.
source: One major obstacle to developing a universal vaccine is the high mutability of HIV (Korber et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Korber et al., 2001

claim: Broadly neutralizing antibodies have shown potential to both prevent new infection in animal models and to control existing infection for some duration in both human and animal models.
source: Antibodies (Abs) that can neutralize a broad diversity of HIV strains, known as broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), are of great interest in this regard because they have shown potential to both prevent new infection in animal models and to control existing infection for some duration in both human and animal models (Barouch et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2012; Mascola et al., 2000; Moldt et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: BnAbs naturally evolve in only a subset of HIV-infected patients, and usually in low titers after several years of infection.
source: BnAbs naturally evolve in only a subset of HIV-infected patients, and usually in low titers after several years of infection.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Past attempts at eliciting bnAbs by vaccination have failed.
source: Past attempts at eliciting them by vaccination have failed (Kong and Sattentau, 2012; McCoy and Weiss, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kong and Sattentau, 2012 and McCoy and Weiss, 2013

claim: A vaccination protocol that can efficiently induce bnAbs in non-human primates or humans is not available.
source: Despite significant progress (Shaffer et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015; Escolano et al., 2016; Steichen et al., 2016; Bonsignori et al., 2016), a vaccination protocol that can efficiently induce bnAbs in non-human primates or humans is not available.
evidence: Stated as current state of the field with citations to recent progress

claim: During affinity maturation, B cells proliferate and mutations are introduced in the receptor at a high rate through somatic hypermutation.
source: During affinity maturation (AM) B cells proliferate, and upon induction of the activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) gene, mutations are introduced in the receptor at a high rate (somatic hypermutation).
evidence: Describes established biological process of affinity maturation

claim: BnAbs exhibit unusual structural features such as a high degree of somatic hypermutation in the complementarity determining regions (CDRs), as well as changes in the surrounding framework regions (FWR).
source: BnAbs exhibit unusual structural features such as a high degree of somatic hypermutation (including insertions and deletions) in the antigen binding regions known as the complementarity determining regions (CDRs), as well as changes in the surrounding framework regions (FWR) (Scheid et al., 2009; Sok et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scheid et al., 2009 and Sok et al., 2013

claim: Klein et al. showed that, for the bnAbs they studied, the reversal of FWR mutations reduces breadth and potency.
source: For example, Klein et al. showed that, for the bnAbs they studied, the reversal of FWR mutations reduces breadth and potency.
evidence: Refers to findings from Klein et al. study

claim: FWR mutations had no effect on non-broadly neutralizing antibodies.
source: However, the FWR mutations had no effect on non-broadly neutralizing antibodies (Klein et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klein et al., 2013

claim: It has been proposed that FWR mutations increase neutralizing breadth by providing the Ab with greater conformational flexibility.
source: it has been proposed that FWR mutations increase neutralizing breadth by providing the Ab with greater conformational flexibility (Scheid et al., 2011; Klein et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scheid et al., 2011 and Klein et al., 2013

claim: A subsequent study of the 4E10 bnAb found a high degree of plasticity in the mature antibody.
source: A subsequent study of the 4E10 bnAb also found a high degree of plasticity in the mature antibody (Finton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Finton et al., 2014

claim: The established paradigm of antibody maturation suggests that antibodies progressively become more rigid as AM ensues.
source: The implications of these studies contradict the established paradigm of antibody maturation, which suggests that antibodies progressively become more rigid as AM ensues (Schmidt et al., 2013; Eisen and Chakraborty, 2010; Foote and Milstein, 1994; Wedemayer et al., 1997; Thorpe and Brooks, 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing the established paradigm

claim: A recent study on a class of enzymes showed that adaptation to different ligands in a PDZ domain preferentially occurred through a collection of distant mutations that worked allosterically to enable multiple conformational states.
source: A recent study on a class of enzymes showed that adaptation to different ligands in a PDZ domain preferentially occurred not only through mutations in the ligand-binding site, but rather through a collection of distant mutations (Raman et al., 2016). These mutations worked allosterically to enable multiple conformational states, therefore allowing binding to a diversity of ligands during adaptation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Raman et al., 2016

claim: The P61A reversal mutation in the heavy chain of 3BNC60 disrupts the secondary structure of the β-sheet connecting the CDR2 and FWR3 regions, resulting in partial unfolding of the region.
source: The results shown in Figure 1A quantify the dramatic effect of the P61A reversal mutation in the heavy chain of 3BNC60. Consistent with experiments, the presence of proline in the mature antibody disrupts the secondary structure of the β-sheet connecting the CDR2 and FWR3 regions, resulting in partial unfolding of the region (Klein et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1A and citation to Klein et al., 2013

claim: The melting temperature for the P61A reverted 3BNC60 mature antibody was 5K lower than that for the mature bnAb.
source: The large RMS fluctuations indicate a more flexible structure, and are thus consistent with the observation that the melting temperature for the P61A reverted 3BNC60 mature antibody was 5K lower than that for the mature bnAb (Klein et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klein et al., 2013

claim: There was a progressive increase in flexibility of the 3BNC60 lineage of antibodies as affinity maturation progressed.
source: From these results we conclude that there was a progressive increase in flexibility of the 3BNC60 lineage of antibodies as affinity maturation progressed.
evidence: Based on conformational entropy calculations shown in Figure 3 and RMSF data

claim: The evolution of flexibility of the heavy chains of the CH103 lineage is opposite to that of 3BNC60, since the antibodies become progressively stiffer as the lineage matures.
source: The evolution of flexibility of the heavy chains of the CH103 lineage is opposite to that of 3BNC60 (Figure 1B), since the antibodies become progressively stiffer as the lineage matures.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 3

claim: Fera et al. attribute the breadth increase in the CH103 lineage to a reorientation of the LC relative to the HC, which alleviates steric clashes with gp120 variants that have longer V5 loops.
source: In fact, (Fera et al., 2014) attribute the breadth increase in the CH103 lineage to a reorientation of the LC relative to the HC, which alleviates steric clashes with gp120 variants that have longer V5 loops.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fera et al., 2014

claim: The variation in flexibility reported for the CH103 lineage is consistent with earlier studies of non-broadly neutralizing antibodies, which also showed a loss of flexibility during maturation.
source: Furthermore, the variation in flexibility that we report for the CH103 lineage is consistent with earlier studies of non-broadly neutralizing antibodies, which also showed a loss of flexibility during maturation (Chong et al., 1999; Thorpe and Brooks, 2007; Wong et al., 2011), and with the traditional paradigm of affinity maturation (Foote and Milstein, 1994; Wedemayer et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: For the PGT121 lineage, flexibility changes are observed in the CDR3 region of the heavy chains.
source: For the PGT121 lineage, our MD simulation results exhibit greater complexity. For the heavy chains of this lineage, flexibility changes are observed in the CDR3 region (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In the PGT121 antibody, CDR3 has a 11 residue insertion relative to the 3BNC60 and CH103 lineages, and is involved in binding to gp120 glycans.
source: In this antibody, CDR3 has a 11 residue insertion relative to the 3BNC60 and CH103 lineages, and is involved in binding to gp120 glycans (Garces et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garces et al., 2015

claim: The intermediate PGT121 construct (3 hr/109L) has high flexibility, particularly in the framework regions.
source: While the mature variant is less flexible than the germline in the regions FWR3-FWR4, the intermediate construct has high flexibility, particularly in the framework regions (see Figure 1F and Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 2B

claim: Both chains of the 3H109L PGT121 intermediate have higher entropies than the corresponding germline and mature structures, with the increase being more pronounced for the light chain.
source: Specifically, both chains of the 3H109L PGT121 intermediate have higher entropies than the corresponding germline and mature structures, with the increase being more pronounced for the light chain (Figure 3), on which we focus below.
evidence: Supported by conformational entropy data shown in Figure 3

claim: In the PGT121 light chain, the FWR3 region near residue 68 is well ordered and interacts with the CDR1 region near residue S27, with hydrogen bonds formed between S27 and G68.
source: In the PGT121 light chain, the FWR3 region near residue 68 is well ordered, and interacts with the CDR1 region near residue S27 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Hydrogen bonds are formed between S27 (both, side chain and backbone oxygens) and G68 (backbone amide).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: In the 109L LC, serine at position 27 is an alanine, and the stabilizing hydrogen bonds do not form, which allows the FWR3 region to unfold locally near the three residue insertion 66(a)P-66(b)D-66(c)I.
source: In the 109L LC the serine is an alanine, and the stabilizing hydrogen bonds do not form, which allows the FWR3 region to unfold locally near the three residue insertion 66(a)P-66(b)D-66(c)I.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of MD simulation data

claim: Flexibility throughout the antibody can be changed significantly by mutations in both the FWR and CDR regions.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that flexibility throughout the antibody can be changed significantly by mutations in both the FWR and CDR regions, and, more generally, that affinity maturation in bnAbs does not follow the rigidification paradigm in all cases.
evidence: Based on MD simulation results for all three lineages

claim: For the 3BNC60 lineage, flexibility progressively increased during affinity maturation.
source: For the 3BNC60 lineage, flexibility progressively increased, while the opposite is true for the CH103 lineage.
evidence: Based on MD simulation results shown in Figures 1 and 3

claim: For the CH103 lineage, flexibility progressively decreased during affinity maturation.
source: For the 3BNC60 lineage, flexibility progressively increased, while the opposite is true for the CH103 lineage.
evidence: Based on MD simulation results shown in Figures 1 and 3

claim: For the PGT121 lineage, the intermediate is more flexible than either the mature or germline antibodies.
source: For the PGT121 lineage, our results indicate that the intermediate is more flexible than either the mature or germline antibodies, so that this is an example of a more complex maturation trajectory.
evidence: Based on MD simulation results shown in Figures 1 and 3

claim: The germline for the CH103 lineage bound strongly to the CD4 binding site of the founder HIV envelope glycoprotein.
source: The germline for the CH103 lineage bound strongly to the CD4 binding site of the founder HIV envelope glycoprotein (Liao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liao et al., 2013

claim: Ancestors of 3BNC60 show lower potency and breadth of neutralization.
source: Conversely, ancestors of 3BNC60 show lower potency and breadth of neutralization (Scheid et al., 2011; Klein et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scheid et al., 2011 and Klein et al., 2013

claim: When the germline BCR binds to the conserved residues with relatively high affinity, B cells evolve CDR and FWR mutations that strengthen the binding energy to the shared conserved residues and reduce the flexibility of the antibody.
source: When the germline B cells bind to the conserved residues with relatively high affinity (e.g., Ec≈ −4), B cells evolve CDR and FWR mutations that strengthen the binding energy (Ec) to the shared conserved residues and reduce the flexibility of the antibody (increase Q); if the initial Q is already high, the increase may be relatively small.
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 4

claim: When the binding energy of the germline B cell to the shared conserved residues is weaker, B cells typically need to acquire FWR mutations that increase their flexibility in order to be able to be positively selected in the presence of multiple variant antigens.
source: In the case where the binding energy of the germline B cell to the shared conserved residues is weaker (taken to be Ec = 0), we find that B cells typically need to acquire FWR mutations that increase their flexibility in order to be able to be positively selected in the presence of multiple variant antigens (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 4

claim: In simulations where changes to flexibility are disallowed, GC reactions are 35% less likely to complete successfully because all the B cells undergo apoptosis as AM ensues.
source: This is made evident by the fact that in simulations where changes to flexibility are disallowed, GC reactions are 35% less likely to complete successfully because all the B cells undergo apoptosis as AM ensues (data not shown).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations

claim: If the evolutionary trajectories progress beyond a reasonably favorable value of Ec, then framework mutations that make the structure more rigid are acquired.
source: Figure 4A shows that, in the case where germline B cells have a weak binding energy Ec, if the evolutionary trajectories progress beyond a reasonably favorable value of Ec (which our simulations show to be roughly equal to E0), then framework mutations that make the structure more rigid are acquired much like the case where germline B cells exhibit a stronger Ec.
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 4A

claim: The population that exhibits lower breadth and lower final values of Ec is comprised of those antibodies that are more flexible, while those that continue to evolve and become more rigid have a higher breadth and potency.
source: Analyses of our results demonstrate that the population that exhibits lower breadth (median binding free energy) and lower final values of Ec is comprised of those antibodies that are more flexible, while those that continue to evolve and become more rigid have a higher breadth and potency (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 4C

claim: The reason that PGT121 is more potent than 3BNC60 is likely that it has proceeded further along the evolutionary trajectory and become more rigid.
source: This is observed in our simulations once Ec is sufficiently high that Ew <E0; conformational plasticity is now no longer required and the selection pressure will increase Q to enhance the effect of the first term in Equation 1b. This phenomenon is consistent with the AM trajectories of the PGT121 lineage (purple curve). The reason that PGT121 is more potent than 3BNC60 is likely that it has proceeded further along the evolutionary trajectory and become more rigid.
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations and comparison with MD results

claim: Antibodies that start with a relatively strong binding with the conserved region (CH103-like) accumulate mostly affinity-improving CDR mutations while some FWR mutations contribute to rigidity.
source: Antibodies that start with a relatively strong binding with the conserved region (CH103-like) accumulate mostly affinity-improving CDR mutations while some FWR mutations contribute to rigidity (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 6A

claim: Antibodies that start with weaker binding to the conserved region (PGT121- and 3BNC60-like) more rapidly accumulate FWR mutations that improve flexibility during the early stages of AM.
source: In contrast, antibodies that start with weaker binding to the conserved region (PGT121- and 3BNC60-like) more rapidly accumulate FWR mutations that improve flexibility during the early stages of AM (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 6B

claim: A phylogenetic analysis of antibodies from the 3BNC60 lineage places two important FWR mutations near the root, suggesting that they emerged early during the developmental process.
source: This is a prediction of our model which is supported by experimental results from (Klein et al., 2013) where a phylogenetic analysis of antibodies from the 3BNC60 lineage places two important FWR mutations near the root, suggesting that they emerged early during the developmental process.
evidence: Supported by citation to Klein et al., 2013

claim: If germline B cells can be activated that bind sufficiently strongly to the shared conserved residues of a target epitope, there is no need for the subsequent immunization with variant immunogens to induce FWR mutations that increase flexibility of the BCRs as AM ensues.
source: If germline B cells can be activated that bind sufficiently strongly to the shared conserved residues of a target epitope of a class of bnAbs (e.g., the CD4 binding site), there is no need for the subsequent immunization with variant immunogens to induce FWR mutations that increase flexibility of the BCRs as AM ensues.
evidence: Based on inference from affinity maturation model results

claim: Strategies that result in inducing germline B cells that bind strongly to conserved residues would considerably simplify the design of boosting immunogens.
source: Thus, our results suggest that strategies that result in inducing such germline B cells (Steichen et al., 2016; Escolano et al., 2016; Jardine et al., 2016; Jardine et al., 2015; Jardine et al., 2013) would considerably simplify the design of boosting immunogens.
evidence: Based on inference from model results with citations to relevant strategies

claim: The CHARMM36 energy function was used for the MD simulations.
source: The CHARMM36 energy function was used for the MD simulations.
evidence: Methodological detail stated in Materials and methods

claim: Five 100ns trajectories were generated for each structure, starting from different initial conditions.
source: We generated five 100ns trajectories for each structure, starting from different initial conditions (velocities; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Methodological detail stated in the manuscript

claim: Each B cell divides twice per GC cycle (four divisions per day).
source: each B cell of the dark zone divides twice per GC cycle (four divisions per day) (Zhang and Shakhnovich, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang and Shakhnovich, 2010

claim: A mutation occurs with a probability of 0.20 per sequence per division during somatic hypermutation.
source: and a mutation occurs with a probability of 0.20 per sequence per division (Berek and Milstein, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berek and Milstein, 1987

claim: Mutational hotspots have mostly been found in the CDR regions.
source: Although the FWR constitutes over two thirds of the variable domain by sequence, mutational hotspots have mostly been found in the CDR (Neuberger and Milstein, 1995; Tomlinson et al., 1996; Wagner and Neuberger, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Neuberger and Milstein, 1995; Tomlinson et al., 1996; Wagner and Neuberger, 1996

claim: Apoptosis occurs half of the time for CDR mutations, 30% of mutations are silent, and 20% are binding energy-affecting mutations.
source: The probability that a CDR mutation will follow one of these paths is governed by probabilities obtained from experiments (Berek and Milstein, 1987). Apoptosis occurs half of the time, 30% of mutations are silent, and 20% are binding energy-affecting mutations (Zhang and Shakhnovich, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berek and Milstein, 1987 and Zhang and Shakhnovich, 2010

claim: Binding energy-affecting mutations are more likely to be deleterious than advantageous.
source: Experimental studies of protein-protein interactions indicate that binding energy-affecting mutations are more likely to be deleterious than advantageous (Moal and Fernández-Recio, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moal and Fernández-Recio, 2012

claim: If B cells interact with multiple variants of the antigen in every cycle, bnAbs are less likely to evolve.
source: It was shown previously that, if B cells interact with multiple variants of the antigen in every cycle, bnAbs are less likely to evolve (Wang et al., 2015; Shaffer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2015 and Shaffer et al., 2016

claim: The model reproduces experimentally observed order-of-magnitude increases in the binding affinity during AM induced by a single antigen.
source: Although the model that we simulate lacks structural detail, it reproduces experimentally observed order-of-magnitude increases in the binding affinity during AM induced by a single antigen (see Materials and methods and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Diversification of viral strains often precedes the development of bnAbs in infected persons.
source: Past studies analyzing the evolution of bnAbs in infected persons show that often diversification of viral strains precedes the development of bnAbs (Liao et al., 2013; Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Bhiman et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liao et al., 2013; Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Bhiman et al., 2015

claim: 3BNC117 is slightly more potent than CH103.
source: Although we could not find specific comparative data for 3BNC60, another 3B class of bnAb, 3BNC117, is slightly more potent than CH103 (Chuang et al., 2013; Eroshkin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chuang et al., 2013 and Eroshkin et al., 2014

claim: 3BNC55 is less potent than CH103.
source: Indirect comparisons based on available data (Scheid et al., 2011; Chuang et al., 2013) suggest that 3BNC55, another bnAb with the P61 FWR mutation is less potent than CH103.
evidence: Based on inference from cited data

claim: The conformational entropy from quasi-harmonic analysis typically overestimates the true conformational entropy.
source: Although it is known that the conformational entropy from quasi-harmonic analysis typically overestimates the true conformational entropy (see, e.g., [Tyka et al., 2007]), the relative differences between the structures studied are expected to be meaningful because of the overall structure similarity of antibodies in the same lineage.
evidence: Supported by citation to Tyka et al., 2007

claim: The constant and variable regions of antibodies remained well-separated in simulations including both regions.
source: To ensure that the truncation of the antibody constant regions would not impact the conclusions of this study, we also simulated by MD the 3BNC60 antibodies without truncation (i.e. including both the variable and constant regions, for 400ns for each structure. In these simulations, the constant and variable regions remained well-separated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) suggesting that the interactions between them were relatively weak.
evidence: Based on MD simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The qualitative results of the affinity maturation model are robust to some variation in the parameters.
source: Consistent with the qualitative nature of the model, we did not attempt to choose an 'optimal' set of parameters, for example by precisely fitting the typical number of mutations or GC duration in the single antigen case. A strength of our model is that the qualitative results are robust to some variation in the parameters.
evidence: Statement about model robustness based on simulation results

claim: The same qualitative maturation pathways are observed in simulations with λ = 0.8 as with λ = 0.9.
source: We find that the same qualitative maturation pathways are also observed in these simulations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Due to greater dissimilarity between antigens with λ = 0.8, there is stronger selection for flexibility (lower Q).
source: However, due to the greater dissimilarity between antigens against which the Abs mature, there is stronger selection for flexibility (lower Q).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations with λ = 0.8

claim: Shifting E0 to very strong or weak binding energies affects the preferred antibody maturation pathway when the germline B cell does not bind strongly to the conserved residues of the epitope.
source: We have explored the effects of varying the value of this parameter on our results when the germline B cell does not bind strongly to the conserved residues of the epitope (weak initial Ec). As Figure 4—figure supplement 3 shows, shifting E0 to very strong or weak binding energies affects the preferred antibody maturation pathway.
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: A significantly more favorable value of E0 makes flexibility-increasing framework mutations more beneficial and drives antibody evolution more along 3BNC60-like trajectories.
source: A significantly more favorable value of E0 than that used to obtain the results in Figure 4 makes flexibility-increasing framework mutations more beneficial, and thus drives antibody evolution more along 3BNC60-like trajectories (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 3 with Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: If E0 is weaker than what was used to obtain the results in Figure 4 and the same antigen concentration is used, most of the B cells die and the GC is likely to be extinguished.
source: If E0 is weaker than what was used to obtain the results in Figure 4, and we use the same antigen concentration as before, most of the B cells die and the GC is likely to be extinguished.
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations

claim: When E0 is weak and antigen concentration is increased, more CH103-like maturation trajectories are promoted.
source: In this circumstance, if the antigen concentration is increased, we find that the GCs are not extinguished with high probability, and more CH103-like maturation trajectories are promoted (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 3 with Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Varying values of E0 change the rate of acquiring CDR versus FWR mutations.
source: Consistent with the points noted above, varying values of E0 also change the rate of acquiring CDR versus FWR mutations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), with stronger values of E0 promoting FWR mutations more than in Figure 6B and weaker values of E0 suppressing FWR mutations.
evidence: Based on affinity maturation model simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1
